hints: Focus on polarity first, because any polar bond or hydrogen bonding means there will be stronger forces in addition to dispersion forces.
Notice that water and methanol both contain O-H groups, while hydrogen chloride is a polar diatomic molecule.
Think about which listed substance is a non-polar hydrocarbon with only C-C and C-H bonds, so no permanent dipoles or hydrogen bonds are possible.
walkthrough:
**Recall the types of intermolecular force**

All molecules have temporary dipole-induced dipole attractions, also called London dispersion forces. Polar molecules have permanent dipole-dipole forces as well, and molecules with H bonded to N, O or F also have hydrogen bonding.

Rule to use:
$$\text{non-polar molecule = London forces only, polar molecule = London + permanent dipole, H-O/N/F = London + hydrogen bond}$$

**Test the polar and hydrogen-bonding substances**

$\text{HCl}$ is polar due to the electronegativity difference between H and Cl, so it has permanent dipole-dipole forces. $\text{CH}_3\text{OH}$ and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ both contain O-H groups, so they have hydrogen bonding plus London forces.

**Identify the non-polar hydrocarbon**

Octane, $\text{C}_8\text{H}_{18}$, is an alkane with only C-C and C-H bonds. These bonds are essentially non-polar, so the molecule has no permanent dipole and cannot hydrogen bond. Therefore the only intermolecular forces between octane molecules are temporary dipole-induced dipole attractions.

options.A: Incorrect. Hydrogen chloride, $\text{HCl}$, is polar because chlorine is much more electronegative than hydrogen. It has permanent dipole-dipole attractions in addition to London forces.
options.B: Incorrect. Methanol, $\text{CH}_3\text{OH}$, contains an O-H group so it forms hydrogen bonds. It has both hydrogen bonding and London forces, not London forces only.
options.C: Correct. Octane, $\text{C}_8\text{H}_{18}$, is a non-polar alkane. With only C-C and C-H bonds and no O-H, N-H or polar bonds, it cannot form hydrogen bonds or permanent dipole-dipole forces, so only temporary dipole-induced dipole attractions act between molecules.
options.D: Incorrect. Water, $\text{H}_2\text{O}$, has two O-H bonds and lone pairs on oxygen, so it forms strong hydrogen bonds. This is a classic trap if you forget that London forces are present but are not the only force.
